newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Depressed Russian region despairs of reform.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Depressed Russian region despairs of reform.

text.p: At 35, Igor Minyazhetdinov is a couple of years younger than Boris Nemtsov, the boyish reformer President Boris Yeltsin has charged with shaking Russia from the vestiges of Soviet economic planning.

Yet 18 months struggling to save a bankrupt 19th-century cotton mill in a forgotten village in one of the regions hardest hit by free market reforms has left Igor and many like him aged beyond his years and disillusioned with the government.
"Moscow doesn't give a damn about us. They just want their taxes. But unless they let us get back on our feet this village is just going to die," he told Reuters.

Nearly 700 of the Krasny Dulyapinets Cloth Works' 750 staff have been laid off, leaving almost every adult in Dulyapino out of work. Those left to maintain the mill, paid from sales of stock and lumber from factory land, get $20 a month on average.

When Minyazhetdinov's predecessor hanged himself, local officials turned to the stocky, fast-talking ethnic Tatar, who had a career in cotton mills in the surrounding Ivanovo region, northeast of Moscow. Yeltsin, who has demanded more young leaders to pull Russia out of crisis, might have approved.

But the manager's experience and conditions in the region -- an April survey showed two-thirds of people living below a breadline set at $60 a month -- highlight a gulf between Kremlin comments that growth is coming and the reality of five years in which output has halved and jobs for all are a distant memory.
DEBT BURDEN THWARTS INITIATIVE

Minyazhetdinov complains, as he sits in a chilly Dickensian office above rows of silent looms in crumbling red-brick workshops, that the state owners have vetoed cash for every scheme to revive the plant -- from making pasta to weaving silk.

Nemtsov, until March governor of the neighbouring Nizhny Novgorod region, and fellow first deputy prime minister Anatoly Chubais have made plugging a huge budget gap their priority and say there is no cash or debt write-offs for lame duck firms.

It is hard on the textile industry. The end of the Soviet Union cost it cheap Uzbek cotton and its market in the garment factories of Ukraine. The Uzbeks sell their cotton on the world market and Russian shops are full of cheap clothes from Asia.

Krasny Dulyapinets, like the dozens of mills around Ivanovo which once wove much of the Soviet Union's cotton cloth, has been at a standstill for three years. It owes $1 million, mainly to the state and state energy firms, and the bills are mounting.
Minyazhetdinov sees little prospect of paying it back or rehiring much of the workforce, but insists even a small credit would get the plant -- and the village -- doing something again.

"The people want to work. I want to feed my workers. This is a very viable plant. But it needs investment," he said. Yet he adds that little more than pride -- and a long-term plan to farm mushrooms in old factory buildings -- prevented him giving up.
"Yeltsin has no plan. Moscow treats people like cattle. They should understand people here have no meat."
JOBLESS WORKERS SURVIVE ON POTATOES
"Like most people here, we get by on potatoes and vegetables we can grow ourselves," said 43-yearold Yakov, who worked at the plant for 20 years until 1994. "People are hungry."
A Georgian from the south, his native good humour has turned bitter with the strain of bringing up three children on his and his wife's combined unemployment benefit of $25 a month.

"This was a good place to live. Now, we have no future," he said, surveying cottages huddled round the mill founded in 1861. But with most of Russia in crisis and long distances between towns, Yakov and his neighbours feel they have nowhere to go.
At the village hall, communist deputy mayer Lev Kochatev, a pensioner from the factory, shared his pessimism.

"I honestly don't know how some of our people get by," he said. The luckiest have a pensioner in the family, though even state pensions are months overdue. "I know that mill and I know it'll take a lot of money to get it going. But from where?"
The 2,000 folk of Dulyapino produced only three babies last year. But 43 people died. "If we don't re-establish our industry, we're just going to disappear," Kochatev said.
LOCAL LEADERS SEE SOME HOPE
The only people moving in to Dulyapino these days are a few more prosperous city folk from Ivanovo, 40 km (25 miles) away, who are buying up traditional wooden cottages as holiday homes.

Officials in the regional capital, as in Moscow, say things are looking up. Governor Vladislav Tikhomirov told the local newspaper that output in the first quarter was 7.2 percent more than a year ago and said he had assurances from Nemtsov that local industry's demand for tax relief was being considered.

Yet at the regional employment office, deputy director Boris Lepilov admitted promising signs can mask a worsening problem. Official unemployment in the Ivanovo region fell by a quarter last year to stand at 9.5 percent. Having had one of the highest rates in Russia, it is now in line with the national average.

But, Lepilov noted, many have dropped off the roll because their entitlement has run out. Others do not bother to claim. For a year, the system has had almost no funding, so claimants get only around $15 a month, if that. Some receive food instead.
"PEOPLE ARE FRIGHTENINGLY PATIENT"

For all the slump in their living standards, the mill workers of Ivanovo, who staged Russia's first industrial strike in 1897 and formed the first soviet (workers' council) during the failed 1905 revolution, have maintained a virtual silence.
"People are frighteningly patient," remarked Lepilov.
Some 20,000 marched during a national protest in March. But even some of its organisers see it as a waste of time.
"People could strike for weeks and make no difference. They have no work anyway," said Vladimir Cherkashov, 40, a cotton worker and parliamentary candidate for the Union of Labour.
"It's true some of the old communist bosses' only idea of capitalism is filling their pockets, but there are bosses with ideas and we need to work together to save our industry.
"People are always telling me 'Give us Kalashnikovs!'" Cherkashov said. "But there'll be no revolution. Russians know what that means and they don't want bloodshed. They're patient."

A sense that neither capitalism nor communism is the answer is common in Ivanovo. It gave General Alexander Lebed one of his best results in the 1996 presidential election, matching Yeltsin on 30 percent and well ahead of the communist candidate.

"Nemtsov seems a good lad," said Alexander Vasyuk, 40, a plumber at Ivanovo's Dzerzhinsky textile plant. "But we need a strong man like Lebed to get those crooks in Moscow off our backs," he said into the gloom of the cramped factory-owned room where he, his wife and three children get by on $50 a month.
